Its not about a warrant, the FBI got a court order sent to Apple to create a a way to open all encrypted phones. A warrant would apply to a single unit, the backdoor would apply to all phones.

The problem is, once its made to where that door can be opened either by knocking it down or with a special key there is nothing stopping anyone else from knocking down the door or using that special key. Right now, Apple can't break the encryption on the phone. They designed it that way to it can't get compromised by thieves or anyone else. The same data on your phone is easily available to law enforcement (also potentially hackers) if its backed up to your iCloud account.

If Apple develops a way to beat the encryption that they developed to specifically not be defeated it will open the door for other people to do it because they know a way exists. So, law enforcement can get a warrant from a judge to access your house either with the right key or by breaking down the door and get to whatever they want inside. With encryption, its like if all the stuff in your house doesn't even exist until you put your specific key in the door. All your stuff is safe as long as you lock up. No one can get to it unless they have your key. If the government forces lock makers to make a master key for that lock, every thief, hacker and unscrupulous person will be after a copy of that key and they will get it. Thieves and hackers don't usually get a warrant to break in and steal your stuff.

This isn't about searching the phone, this is about technology and encryption. Law enforcement already routinely obtain and act on warrants to search cellphone contents. That's all perfectly legal. Starting with iOS 8, Apple implemented security features and encryption on their phones with the intention of making users' personal info more secure from criminals, primarily so they could make their Apple Pay payment network safer and more attractive to banks, credit card companies and consumers. A side-effect of these security features, especially its strong encryption, was that it made the jobs of law enforcement and intelligence agencies much more difficult. The FBI is now seeking ways to bypass this encryption so they can have access to all this personal information. However, technologically speaking, what they want is not possible, and they refuse to accept that. To create a "backdoor" in encryption would totally break that encryption and make it useless. It simply is not technologically possible, nor mathematically possible, to create secure encryption that also has a backdoor. It simply isn't possible. This backdoor would be found and used by governments good AND bad, criminals and anyone else with the skills.

And remember, the FBI and law enforcement already can get legal access to most info on an iPhone or any phone. Cellphone carriers like Verizon are all legally bound to provide call records; and app companies' user records can be subpoenaed. Not to mention all the other routes law enforcement now has to legally obtain data like location with fitness trackers, smartwatches, learning thermostats, etc. That again is why this is about the technology of encryption, not searching a specific phone.

This is all muddied because the courts and law enforcement are making this a legal argument when it is in fact a technology and math issue. And it is ironic, because it could be argued that the USA has the most to gain by having the most secure (best encrypted) technology and also the most to lose by having compromise/broken encryption. Make no mistake, if secure encryption is made to be given a backdoor, it is automatically insecure for everyone.
